decision.explanation: An antiderivative of 5xe^{x^2} is (5/2)e^{x^2}. Evaluating at the bounds gives (5/2)(e^{ln 3}-e^0)=(5/2)(3-1)=5.

after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}}5x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}}5{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}5{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(3-1) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(2) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the integral ∫x7x2−7dx.

a
 2⋅7x2−7ln⁡7+C
b
 7x2−72ln⁡7+C
c
 7x2−7+C
d
 7x2−7ln⁡72+C

 7x2−72+C

decision.explanation: Set u=x^2−7, giving du=2x dx. Then the integral is (1/2)∫7^u du=7^u/(2 ln 7)+C. Substituting back matches option b.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={x}^{2}-7.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{7}^{{x}^{2}-7}\,\text{d}x & =\int {7}^{{x}^{2}-7}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {7}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {7}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{{7}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡7}+C \\  & =\frac{{7}^{{x}^{2}-7}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the integral ∫x7x2−7dx.

a
 2⋅7x2−7ln⁡7+C
b

c

d

EXPLANATION

Let's introduce the new variable u=x2−7. Differentiating gives dudx=2x⟹12du=xdx.

Therefore,

∫x7x2−7dx=∫7x2−7⋅xdx=∫7u⋅12du=12∫7udu=127uln⁡7+C=7x2−72ln⁡7+C.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option b. With u=x^2−7 and x dx=du/2, the integral is 7^{x^2−7}/(2 ln 7)+C. Differentiating this expression gives the original integrand.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing Other Exponential Functions
content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={x}^{2}-7.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{7}^{{x}^{2}-7}\,\text{d}x & =\int {7}^{{x}^{2}-7}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {7}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {7}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{{7}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡7}+C \\  & =\frac{{7}^{{x}^{2}-7}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ | $4\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}x{e}^{3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}({e}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(16-2) \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
